HUMAN EMOTION RATINGS

EmoSynth

Synthetic sine, square and sawtooth sounds with different frequencies, envelopes and durations. The original study reports 40 annotators using 1–5 valence and arousal scales. Per-sound averages describe perceived emotion, not personal liking or clinical outcomes.

Source: Baird, Parada-Cabaleiro, Fraser, Hantke & Schuller (2018), corrected 2020 archive. Our figures and acoustic features are derived analyses.

Dataset & CC BY 4.0 license ↗

CONTROLLED STUDY STIMULI

Birdsong & traffic

A randomized online experiment assigned 295 people to four six-minute soundscapes. Anxiety and paranoia decreased in the birdsong groups. It did not test migraine or isolate a beneficial frequency.

Here we measure 01:00–01:30 of each recording. That excerpt was not independently tested. Traffic is included as a study comparison, not a comfort recommendation.

Study ↗ · Original recordings ↗

01 · FREQUENCY GROUPS

Which tone groups received more positive ratings?

Each point averages the sound-level valence means within one frequency group. The vertical line shows the lowest and highest sound means across its waveform, envelope and duration variants. This spread is not a confidence interval. A higher group average is a clue within this synthetic dataset, not a recommended listening range.

Reading this batch: the highest group mean is near 3,520 Hz (valence 3.82/5), but that group also has high arousal (4.30/5). Near 311 Hz, mean valence is 3.77/5 and arousal 3.43/5. More positive emotion does not automatically mean a calming sound; these are observations within this release.

Hover or tap a group; use arrow keys when the chart is focused.

Frequency is estimated from the audio, grouped by the dataset's frequency index. The corrected archive does not supply a Hz lookup table. Valence: 1 = negative, 5 = positive. All variants remain included.

03 · INSPECT A RECORDING

What is in the sound?

Hover, tap or use arrow keys to inspect a frequency bin.

Channel powers averaged. Each point sums energy within a logarithmic bin; wider bins cover more frequencies. Zero dB is the highest-energy bin in this recording. This is not power per Hz, calibrated loudness, or a benefit score.

WHAT HAS BEEN TESTED FOR MIGRAINE?

Evidence for listening, not a verified frequency library.

A small 2021 pilot followed 20 people using a structured music intervention for three months and reported fewer migraine attacks. With no control group, it cannot establish that music caused the improvement.

Migraine pilot study ↗

A 2020 open-label randomized study compared chosen music plus usual acute migraine care with usual care alone. It reported better short-term pain outcomes. Participants knew their treatment, and the study did not publish an exact reusable playlist or identify a beneficial frequency zone.

Acute migraine study ↗

A controlled study also found no advantage: a 2013 trial assigned 78 adolescents with migraine or tension-type headache to music therapy or an attention-control rhythm program. Music therapy was not superior for headache frequency or intensity. This involved therapist-led sessions, not a playlist. Attention-controlled trial ↗

These studies inform the product hypothesis. They do not validate the EmoSynth tones, the birdsong excerpts, or our generated sounds as migraine treatments.

REPRODUCIBLE & TRACEABLE

Keep the data and the claim together.

EmoSynth labels are kept separate from personal check-ins and study outcomes. No human-response label is invented for the birdsong or traffic excerpts. The original three YouTube references remain on the reference graphs page.

The private repository includes the analysis scripts, source manifests, checksums, aggregate ratings and derived measurements. EmoSynth audio is available under CC BY 4.0. The OSF audio has no explicit reuse license in its metadata, so this site links to it rather than redistributing it.
